# The intersection of two intervals, one-limb bounds

<!-- Generated by docs/tools/reference.py from gen/claims.json, gen/kernels/, include/kairn/gen/bounds.hpp, proofs/gen/, proofs/audit/, results/milestone1/brute/ and docs/tools/reference_operations.py. Do not edit: run python3 docs/tools/reference.py. -->

Kernel `interval_intersection_1` · proved · [all operations](index.md) · [how to read this page](reading.md)

## What it computes

The intersection of two intervals, exactly; the empty set included:

$$Z = X \cap Y.$$

## C++

**Not yet called by the public headers.** No public operation computes this kernel yet.

## Requires

- $X = [x_l, x_u]$ is a canonical interval: the empty set, $x_l = +\infty$ and $x_u = -\infty$, or a nonempty interval, neither bound a NaN, $x_l \le x_u$, $x_l < +\infty$, $x_u > -\infty$, each bound a number of `T` or an infinity; its members are the real numbers between its bounds.
- $Y = [y_l, y_u]$ is a canonical interval: the empty set, $y_l = +\infty$ and $y_u = -\infty$, or a nonempty interval, neither bound a NaN, $y_l \le y_u$, $y_l < +\infty$, $y_u > -\infty$, each bound a number of `T` or an infinity; its members are the real numbers between its bounds.

## Guarantees

For operands that satisfy the requirements, finite, infinite or NaN:

- The result $Z = [z_l, z_u]$ is a canonical interval.
- $Z$ is empty exactly when no real number is a member of both: when an operand is empty, or $\max(x_l, y_l) > \min(x_u, y_u)$.
- Otherwise $Z = X \cap Y$, exactly: $z_l = \max(x_l, y_l)$ and $z_u = \min(x_u, y_u)$; the intersection with the whole line is the other operand.

Proved for every binary format with a precision of at least 1 bit, rounding to nearest with ties to even and with gradual underflow, in the IEEE model, with signed zeros, infinities, NaN and overflow. Both limb types qualify: `double` has 53 bits, `float` has 24 bits.

## Status

**Proved.** Rocq checks the theorem `interval_intersection_1_correct`, in [`proofs/theories/IeeeIntervalExact.v`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/proofs/theories/IeeeIntervalExact.v); the audit of `make -C proofs` prints the axioms its proof depends on (`Print Assumptions interval_intersection_1_correct`, in [`proofs/gen/IeeeAudit.v`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/proofs/gen/IeeeAudit.v)) and finds none beyond the four allowed ([Axioms](#axioms)).

The audit accepts a proof only if every axiom it depends on is one of the four listed in [`proofs/audit/allowed_axioms.txt`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/proofs/audit/allowed_axioms.txt) ([Proofs](../proofs/index.md#the-four-axioms) says what each states):

- `ClassicalDedekindReals.sig_forall_dec`
- `ClassicalDedekindReals.sig_not_dec`
- `FunctionalExtensionality.functional_extensionality_dep`
- `Classical_Prop.classic`

Which of them the proof of `interval_intersection_1_correct` depends on is not copied here: only a run of Rocq computes it. The CI prints it for every push to `main` and every pull request, and keeps what the audit printed as the artifact `proof-audit` of each run of the [Proofs workflow](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/actions/workflows/proofs.yml).

## Source

**Algorithm:** the larger lower bound and the smaller upper bound, the empty set if they cross (Milestone 2 listing). **License:** algorithm and proof: MIT.

## Listing

From [`gen/kernels/interval_intersection_1.kernel`](https://github.com/danielepanozzo/kairn/blob/main/gen/kernels/interval_intersection_1.kernel), the description the C++ and the formal model (`proofs/gen/IeeeModel.v`) are generated from. Each line is one operation of `T`; one that rounds rounds to nearest, and `prod(a, b)` is $\mathrm{RN}(ab)$, written as a fused multiply-add with a zero addend ([the kernel IR](../developer/architecture.md#the-kernel-ir)).

```
# The intersection of two intervals with one-limb bounds (milestone2.md, "One enclosure
# interface"): the larger lower bound and the smaller upper bound, and the empty set when they
# cross, exact. An empty operand, stored as (+inf, -inf), gives a lower bound +inf and an upper
# bound -inf, which cross; the whole line gives the other operand. No bound is a NaN, so that
# le(l, h) is false exactly when they cross. For every precision.

ml = lt(xl, yl)
l  = select(ml, yl, xl)
mu = lt(yu, xu)
h  = select(mu, yu, xu)
ok = le(l, h)
mi = neg(const inf)
zl = select(ok, l, const inf)
zu = select(ok, h, mi)
```
